A factor connects a pattern across samples to a pattern across features. This
tutorial fits three factors to a bundled dataset, turns the fit into a view,
ranks the features behind one factor and plots activity across samples. Start
with a model fitted directly by flashier; no special fitting wrapper is required.

## Fit and extract

GTEx association z-scores are bundled with flashier. Rows are SNP–gene pairs;
columns are tissues.

```{r fit}
library(flashier.utils)
data("gtex", package = "flashier")
set.seed(1)
fit <- flashier::flash(gtex, greedy_Kmax = 3, backfit = TRUE, verbose = 0)
view <- standardize_factors(fit, sample_side = "columns",
                            feature_scale = "association_z_score")
activity <- factor_activity(view)  # samples × factors
effects <- factor_effects(view)    # features × the same factors
dim(activity)
dim(effects)
round(activity[1:3, ], 2)
```

`standardize_factors()` needs two declarations. `sample_side` says which
matrix side holds samples; here tissues are columns. `feature_scale` is a free
text label for what the values measure, such as `"association_z_score"` or
`"log1p_normalized_counts"`. It is recorded, not applied: preprocess before
fitting, because nothing here transforms your data. Rows and columns must have
unique names; an unnamed fit is rejected rather than given made-up IDs.

### What a view holds

```{r view}
names(view)
```

- `activity`: samples × factors matrix. One row per sample.
- `effects`: features × factors matrix with the same factor columns.
- `offset`: per-feature constant added back when reconstructing.
  `tcrossprod(activity, effects)` is the fitted matrix in samples × features
  orientation, so it is the transpose of `gtex` here because samples are
  columns; [Advanced use](advanced-use.html) shows the `sweep()` call that
  adds the offset.
- `manifest`: the recorded declarations and coordinate choice (`scaling`,
  `feature_scale`, `sample_side`, factor IDs), plus a `basis_id` hash so
  results from different coordinates are never mixed by accident.

The default `scaling = "ldf"` splits the fit into unit-norm factors with the
scale placed on the effects side. `"raw"` keeps flashier's own coordinates and
`"rms"` gives each activity column unit root-mean-square. All three reconstruct
the same matrix. A factor's proportion of variance explained (PVE) comes from
`factor_pve(fit)`.

## Interpret one factor

```{r features}
factor_features(view, factor = "F1", select = "largest", n = 5)[,
  c("feature", "estimate")]
```

`select = "largest"` ranks features by effect size within the factor.
`select = "distinctive"` instead ranks the margin to the strongest competing
factor, which separates a program from its neighbours. Effects retain their
sign. A factor's sign can reverse on both sides without changing reconstruction,
so a negative effect does not by itself mean repression.

```{r activity, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
plot_factor_activity(view)
```

The heatmap shows tissue activity in the declared coordinates. These tissues do
not supply donor-level replication. For your own matrix, use metadata summaries
before assigning biological labels.
